questions.q: If the direction cosines of a line are $k$, $k$, $k$, then the value of $k$ is :
questions.solution:
Direction cosines always satisfy

$$l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1.$$

Here $l = m = n = k$, so

$$k^2 + k^2 + k^2 = 1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 3k^2 = 1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad k^2 =  rac13.$$

Therefore

$$k = \pm rac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.$$

Both signs are genuine — they correspond to the two opposite directions along the same line.

questions.q: If the direction cosines of a line are $\dfrac{1}{a}$, $\dfrac{1}{a}$, $\dfrac{1}{a}$, then :
questions.solution:
Apply $l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1$ :

$$ rac{1}{a^2} +  rac{1}{a^2} +  rac{1}{a^2} = 1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad  rac{3}{a^2} = 1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad a^2 = 3.$$

Therefore

$$a = \pm\sqrt{3}.$$

Note that this is an exact value, not a range — the other three options describe intervals, and the condition on direction cosines pins $a$ down completely.

questions.q: The distance of the point $(p, q, r)$ from the $y$-axis is :
questions.solution:
The foot of the perpendicular from $(p, q, r)$ to the $y$-axis is the point $(0, q, 0)$ — moving along the $y$-axis changes only the $y$-coordinate, so the closest point on the axis keeps $q$ and zeroes the rest.

The distance is therefore

$$\sqrt{(p - 0)^2 + (q - q)^2 + (r - 0)^2} = \sqrt{p^2 + r^2}.$$

The general rule: the distance from a coordinate axis is found by **dropping** that axis's own coordinate and taking the root of the sum of the squares of the other two.

questions.q: Two lines with direction ratios $a_{1}, b_{1}, c_{1}$ and $a_{2}, b_{2}, c_{2}$ are perpendicular if:
questions.solution:
Perpendicular means the dot product of the direction vectors is zero: $\mathbf{a_{1}a_{2} + b_{1}b_{2} + c_{1}c_{2} = 0}$.

The first option is the **parallel** condition — equal ratios mean the same heading.

questions.q: Two lines in space are called skew if they:
questions.solution:
Skew lines never meet and never run parallel — they simply pass by each other at different depths, so no single plane contains both.

A road and a flyover crossing above it: on a map they cross, in space they never touch.

questions.q: Find the distance between the points $(1, 2, 3)$ and $(4, 6, 3)$.
questions.solution:
$d = \sqrt{(4-1)^{2} + (6-2)^{2} + (3-3)^{2}} = \sqrt{9 + 16 + 0} = \mathbf{5}$.

The $z$-coordinates match, so this is really a $3$–$4$–$5$ triangle lying flat in a horizontal plane.

questions.q: Find the angle (in degrees) between two lines whose direction ratios are $1, 1, 0$ and $0, 1, 1$.
questions.solution:
$\cos\theta = \dfrac{\left|a_{1}a_{2} + b_{1}b_{2} + c_{1}c_{2}\right|}{\sqrt{a_{1}^{2}+b_{1}^{2}+c_{1}^{2}}\,\sqrt{a_{2}^{2}+b_{2}^{2}+c_{2}^{2}}} = \dfrac{|0 + 1 + 0|}{\sqrt2\,\sqrt2} = \dfrac12$.

$\theta = \mathbf{60°}$.

The modulus is there because a line has no preferred direction: the angle between two lines is always taken as the acute one.

questions.q: Find $\lambda$ if the lines with direction ratios $2, -1, 3$ and $1, \lambda, 2$ are perpendicular.
A line has direction ratios $2, 3, 6$. Find its direction cosine $l$ (the one along the $x$-axis), taking the positive direction, correct to three decimal places.
questions.solution:
The magnitude is $\sqrt{4 + 9 + 36} = 7$.

$l = \dfrac{2}{7} \approx \mathbf{0.286}$ (and $m = \tfrac37$, $n = \tfrac67$).

Dividing the ratios by their magnitude is what turns a heading into cosines.

questions.q: The line $\dfrac{x - 1}{2} = \dfrac{y + 1}{3} = \dfrac{z - 2}{4}$ passes through a point whose $y$-coordinate is $5$. Find its $x$-coordinate.
questions.solution:
Set each ratio equal to $\lambda$: $x = 1 + 2\lambda$, $y = -1 + 3\lambda$, $z = 2 + 4\lambda$.

$y = 5 \Rightarrow -1 + 3\lambda = 5 \Rightarrow \lambda = 2$.

Then $x = 1 + 4 = \mathbf{5}$ (and $z = 10$).

The parameter $\lambda$ is a dial: turn it and you slide along the line.

questions.q: Write the line $\dfrac{x - 2}{3} = \dfrac{y + 1}{2} = \dfrac{z - 4}{-1}$ in vector form, and state a point on it and its direction.
questions.solution:
The Cartesian form hands you both pieces directly.

**A point on the line:** the numbers subtracted from $x$, $y$, $z$ — namely $(2, -1, 4)$.

**The direction:** the denominators — $3, 2, -1$.

$\mathbf{\vec{r} = \left(2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\right) + \lambda\left(3\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}\right)}$.

Watch the signs: $y + 1$ means the point has $y = -1$, not $+1$. That sign is the single most common slip in this chapter.

questions.q: Find the vector and Cartesian equations of the line through $A(3, -2, 1)$ and $B(5, 1, 7)$.
questions.solution:
**Direction:** $\vec{AB} = (5 - 3,\; 1 + 2,\; 7 - 1) = (2, 3, 6)$.

**Vector form:** $\vec{r} = \left(3\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}\right) + \lambda\left(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}\right)$.

**Cartesian form:** $\dfrac{x - 3}{2} = \dfrac{y + 2}{3} = \dfrac{z - 1}{6}$.

**Check:** putting $\lambda = 1$ gives $(5, 1, 7)$, which is $B$. ✓

Either point may be used as the anchor — the line is the same, only the value of $\lambda$ at each point changes.

questions.q: Find the shortest distance between the lines $\vec{r} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + \lambda\left(2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}\right)$ and $\vec{r} = 2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k} + \mu\left(3\hat{i} - 5\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}\right)$.
questions.solution:
With $\vec{r} = \vec{a_1} + \lambda\vec{b_1}$ and $\vec{r} = \vec{a_2} + \mu\vec{b_2}$:

$d = \dfrac{\left|\left(\vec{a_2} - \vec{a_1}\right)\cdot\left(\vec{b_1}\times\vec{b_2}\right)\right|}{\left|\vec{b_1}\times\vec{b_2}\right|}$.

$\vec{a_2} - \vec{a_1} = \hat{i} + 0\hat{j} - \hat{k}$.

$\vec{b_1}\times\vec{b_2} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 3 & -5 & 2 \end{vmatrix}$

$= \hat{i}\left((-1)(2) - (1)(-5)\right) - \hat{j}\left((2)(2) - (1)(3)\right) + \hat{k}\left((2)(-5) - (-1)(3)\right)$

$= 3\hat{i} - \hat{j} - 7\hat{k}$.

**Numerator:** $(1)(3) + (0)(-1) + (-1)(-7) = 3 + 7 = 10$.

**Denominator:** $\sqrt{9 + 1 + 49} = \sqrt{59}$.

$d = \mathbf{\dfrac{10}{\sqrt{59}}} \approx 1.30$ units.

The cross product points along the one direction perpendicular to **both** lines; the numerator measures how far apart they are along exactly that direction.

questions.q: Find the angle between the lines $\dfrac{x}{1} = \dfrac{y}{2} = \dfrac{z}{2}$ and $\dfrac{x}{3} = \dfrac{y}{-4} = \dfrac{z}{0}$.
questions.solution:
Direction ratios: $(1, 2, 2)$ and $(3, -4, 0)$.

Dot product $= 3 - 8 + 0 = -5$.

Magnitudes: $\sqrt{1 + 4 + 4} = 3$ and $\sqrt{9 + 16 + 0} = 5$.

$\cos\theta = \dfrac{|-5|}{3 \times 5} = \dfrac{1}{3}$.

$\theta = \mathbf{\cos^{-1}\dfrac13} \approx 70.5°$.

A zero in the direction ratios is fine — it simply means the line never moves in that coordinate.
